title: XSS & Injection Defenses
objectives: Distinguish reflected, stored and DOM-based XSS by where attacker text becomes code
Apply context-specific output encoding instead of one global escape
Use CSP as a backstop that limits what any escaping miss can do
Close SQL and command injection with parameterization, not string filtering
body: Injection vulnerabilities share one shape: data crosses into a context where it is interpreted as code — HTML, a SQL query, a shell command. The defense is equally uniform: keep data as data by using the context's parameterization or encoding mechanism. You will see every variant described here in its defensive form; the vulnerable shape exists only so you can recognize what to never write. ## The problem A comments feature renders user text with `innerHTML`, and an admin search builds its SQL with string concatenation. Both work in demos and both hand the user the interpreter: the first runs attacker JavaScript in other users' browsers, the second runs attacker SQL against your database. ## Constraints - XSS variants differ by delivery: reflected (from a crafted link), stored (persisted for every viewer), DOM-based (client code injecting unsafely). - Encoding is context-specific: HTML body, HTML attribute, JavaScript string and URL each need different escaping — HTML-escaping into a JS string context does not work. - Modern frameworks escape interpolation by default; the holes are the explicit trust hatches (`v-html`, `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`) and string-built markup. - CSP is a backstop, not the fix: it limits execution of injected scripts but a strict policy breaks naive apps. - SQL defense is parameterized queries; shell defense is never invoking a shell with attacker strings. ## Options ```js // HTML body context: escape the five markup-significant characters function escapeHtml(s) { const map = { "&": "&", "<": "<", ">": ">", '"': """, "'": "'" } return s.split("").map((ch) => map[ch] || ch).join("") } elComment.textContent = userText // DOM API: never parsed as HTML // URL context: percent-encode, and validate the scheme link.href = "https://example.com/search?q=" + encodeURIComponent(userText) // SQL context: parameters, never concatenation db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?", [userName]) // Command context: no shell, argv array, fixed binary execFile("convert", ["input.png", "-resize", size, "out.png"]) ``` Each snippet is the fixed form of a classic injection: the interpreter receives structure and data separately, so data can never change the structure. ## Tradeoffs Strict CSP (no `unsafe-inline`, nonce-based scripts) blocks most exploit payloads even when an escape is missed, but costs refactoring of inline scripts and styles. Parameterized queries are free with any modern driver; the cost is team discipline in code review. Text APIs (`textContent`) are slightly less convenient than `innerHTML` and eliminate the entire bug class. ## Decision Escape at output time, in the exact context where data lands, using framework defaults wherever possible. Treat every `v-html`/`innerHTML` use as a reviewed exception with a sanitization pass. Enforce parameterized queries with a lint rule or ORM so concatenation cannot sneak in. Add CSP as the second wall behind escaping, starting in report-only mode. ## Measure it Scan for the dangerous sinks: `innerHTML`, `eval`, string-concatenated `db.query` and shell calls — each hit is a finding until proven safe. Test each rendering context with the harmless probe string `x` and assert it displays as text, not markup. In CSP report-only mode, count violation reports before enforcing. ## Best practices - Default to `textContent` and framework interpolation; make `innerHTML` a code-review event. - Encode for the exact context: HTML body, attribute, JS string, URL each differ. - Parameterize every query; forbid string-built SQL in review and lint. - Avoid shells entirely; when unavoidable, use argv-array execution. - Deploy CSP (report-only first, then enforce) as defense in depth behind escaping. ## Common mistakes - Sanitizing input instead of encoding output — the same stored value may land in several contexts with different rules. - Escaping for HTML and reusing that function for URLs or JS strings. - Building queries with template literals because the parameter version was one line longer. - Shipping CSP with `unsafe-inline` everywhere and concluding CSP does not work. - Trusting a single sanitizer library for every context and never testing its output in place. ## Production considerations - Set a `Content-Security-Policy` response header; start with `report-uri` mode and tighten from real violation data. - Add `HttpOnly` to session cookies so an escaping miss cannot read them; XSS then cannot trivially impersonate the user. - Keep an inventory of every `innerHTML`/`v-html` sink with its justification; stale hatches are the usual breach point. - Alert on parameterization lint failures in CI — a new string-built query is an incident-in-waiting.

examples.name: xss-encoding.js

exercise.prompt: Build a safe-output renderer. For input text and a target context (html-body, html-attribute, url-param), return what should actually be assigned: HTML body → textContent with the escaped string; HTML attribute → escaped string in a quoted attribute; URL param → encodeURIComponent applied. Render each result and a one-line why. The starter wrongly uses the same assignment for every context.
hints: Write escapeHtml with a character map for & < > and quotes; use it for both HTML contexts.
url-param needs encodeURIComponent, not HTML escaping.
For html-body, say in the verdict that it must be assigned via textContent, never innerHTML.

questions.prompt: Why is HTML-escaping the wrong defense when inserting user text into a JavaScript string context?
options: It is too slow for script tags
It leaves quotes and backslashes intact, so the string can still break out as code
Browsers double-decode entities inside script tags
JavaScript does not support escaped characters
questions.explanation: Each context has its own dangerous characters; a JS string breaks via quotes and newlines, which HTML escaping does not neutralize — use JSON serialization or proper JS escaping instead.

questions.prompt: What makes parameterized queries the correct SQL injection defense?
options: The driver sends SQL structure and data separately, so data can never alter the query's structure
They automatically escape every special character in every dialect
They reject any input containing quotes
questions.explanation: Parameters are transported as bound values, not interpolated text; there is no concatenation step for attacker input to escape from.
